name: BigCommerce
tagline: Build a small catalog and hand off payments to Stripe Checkout

tiers.name: Core
tiers.limits: Up to $30,000 trailing-12-month GMV before automatic upgrade; unlimited products/bandwidth/staff; 2% open-payment-provider fee; up to 3 storefronts.

tiers.name: Growth
tiers.limits: Up to $100,000 trailing-12-month GMV before automatic upgrade; unlimited products/bandwidth/staff; 1% provider fee; up to 5 storefronts.

tiers.name: Scale
tiers.limits: $33,333 monthly GMV allowance; 0.9% overage on excess; automatic upgrade at $2 million trailing-12-month GMV; 0.6% provider fee; up to 8 storefronts.

tiers.name: Performance
tiers.limits: Starts at $1,499/month billed annually; custom GMV/payment terms; official update cites a $250,000/month Inclusive-GMV reference cap with 0.6% overage above it, subject to contract.
tiers.notes: Custom quote; annual contract; contracted terms control.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 15-day trial with no credit card
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual for Core/Growth/Scale; Performance starts at $1,499/month billed annually
pricing.hiddenCosts: Revenue thresholds force automatic upgrades; Scale charges 0.9% of monthly GMV above $33,333; the Performance update cites a $250,000/month Inclusive-GMV reference cap with 0.6% overage, subject to contract; open-payment-provider fees are 2%/1%/0.6% on Core/Growth/Scale; extra storefronts are $30/$50/$100 per month, and Core phone support is a paid add-on with no public price.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For BigCommerce, build a small catalog and hand off payments to Stripe Checkout. The hard boundary is hosted commerce engine, tax, channels, integrations, scale, and support, plus payments, tax, distribution, and operations.
coreLoopDIY: Sell a small catalog from a user-owned storefront, hand off payments to Stripe Checkout, deliver purchased files or lessons, and manage customers.
whatYouLose: hosted commerce engine, tax, channels, integrations, scale, and support
ongoingBurden: checkout, webhooks, tax, refunds, fraud, entitlements, storage, email, accessibility, backups, and customer support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for BigCommerce because creators pay to outsource the dangerous and tedious parts around money, delivery, tax, and customer access. The recurring cost buys checkout, webhooks, tax, refunds, fraud, entitlements, storage, email, accessibility, backups, and customer support, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Medusa
priorArt.desc: Active open-source commerce platform with modular checkout and fulfillment primitives.

alternatives.name: OpenCart
alternatives.desc: A complete catalog and checkout instead of a small one; free software, paid server chores.

facts.install: Upload a stable PHP release to hosting, create a database, then complete the browser installer
facts.dataFormat: Catalog, customers and orders in a SQL database; images, downloads and application storage in server directories
facts.gapVsPaid: OpenCart replaces managed reliability and integrations with PHP-server administration and a less polished merchant workflow.
facts.setupBlocker: PHP hosting, database and permissions work come first, followed by payment, shipping, mail and extension configuration

alternatives.name: Square Online
alternatives.desc: A free hosted catalog with unlimited products and checkout; it is Square Checkout, not Stripe Checkout.

facts.install: Create a Square account and website from Square Dashboard
facts.dataFormat: Catalog, site content, customers, orders and payments in Square's managed cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: Square Online uses Square rather than Stripe Checkout and offers less catalog, integration and operational depth than BigCommerce.
facts.setupBlocker: A verified Square business account in a supported country is required, and checkout remains tied to Square

alternatives.name: Square Payment Links
alternatives.desc: Embeddable buy buttons and hosted checkout with no monthly bill; country availability is the catch.

facts.install: Create a verified Square account, then build a checkout link or buy button in Square Dashboard
facts.dataFormat: Products, checkout links, customers, orders and payments in Square's managed cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: Square Payment Links is not a real catalog, storefront or order-operations system, and checkout is Square rather than Stripe.
facts.setupBlocker: Only supported Square countries qualify, business verification is required, and every sale incurs Square processing fees

alternatives.name: Stripe Payment Links
alternatives.desc: A tiny product catalog with hosted Stripe checkout; no monthly fee, only ordinary payment processing.

facts.install: Create a Stripe account and Payment Link in Dashboard; API use is optional
facts.dataFormat: Products, prices, links, Checkout Sessions, customers and payments in Stripe's managed cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: Stripe Payment Links supplies only a minimal product list and hosted checkout, not BigCommerce's storefront, catalog management, merchandising and operations.
facts.setupBlocker: A supported-country Stripe business account and verification are required, and ordinary payment-processing fees still apply

alternatives.name: Vvveb
alternatives.desc: A visual catalog, checkout and order desk in one install; much more shop than this brief requires.

facts.install: Download and upload the PHP release, open the site URL, and complete the browser installer
facts.dataFormat: Content, products, orders and settings in MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite or PostgreSQL; media and downloadable files on the server filesystem
facts.gapVsPaid: Vvveb is less mature in catalog operations, integrations, analytics and managed reliability, while still requiring a server.
facts.setupBlocker: PHP hosting, a database, writable files, mail and payment configuration, plus ongoing server updates

alternatives.name: WooCommerce
alternatives.desc: A full WordPress shop for a brief that only asked for a catalog; overkill is still a replacement.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Medusa
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A useful commerce backend for developers, not a catalog-and-checkout product a normal merchant can adopt.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Standard plan and a single-creator storefront DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for BigCommerce in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, Stripe Checkout, and S3-compatible storage; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: sell a small catalog from a user-owned storefront, hand off payments to Stripe Checkout, deliver purchased files or lessons, and manage customers.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement products, variants, prices, files or lessons, coupons, customers, orders, and entitlements.
Use Stripe-hosted Checkout and verify every webhook signature and idempotency key.
Grant access only after confirmed payment and revoke it on refund or chargeback.
Create a customer library with signed short-lived download or lesson URLs.
Add order search, resend receipt, refund handoff, export, and an immutable event log.
Document taxes as the creator's responsibility and do not calculate unsupported jurisdictions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out merchant-of-record tax remittance.
Deliberately leave out a buyer marketplace or affiliate network.
Deliberately leave out advanced communities, certificates, mobile apps, and enterprise learning features.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
